The Rich Fool
FOOL
noun phrase
From Greek aphron, “without reason, senseless,” the parable of the man whose soul was required of him in the night.

📖 Biblical Definition

When one besought our Lord to bid his brother divide the inheritance, Christ warned, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth (Luk 12:15); and He told a parable. The ground of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully, and he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits? (Luk 12:17). He resolved to pull down his barns and build greater, and to lay up all his goods, and said to his soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry (Luk 12:19). But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? (Luk 12:20). The dictionary marks this parable as our Lord’s exposure of covetousness, that practical atheism which lays up treasure for self and is not rich toward God. The rich man’s folly was not in his harvest but in his heart: he reckoned without God, without death, and without his soul. So the Scripture teaches that the abundance of this life cannot secure it, and that a sudden summons may strip the covetous of all. So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God (Luk 12:21).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The parable of the prosperous man whose soul was required the same night, exposing the folly of covetousness.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A parable little redefined by the present age; the principle to recover is that covetousness is folly and a man must be rich toward God.

expand to see more

The parable of the rich fool has drawn little redefinition from the present age, though its warning is little heeded in an age that measures life by abundance. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark our Lord’s plain judgment upon the covetous heart, which lays up treasure for self and reckons without God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that covetousness is folly in the sight of God, and a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth. The rich man’s sin was not his harvest but his heart: he counted his soul his own, his years secured, his goods enough, and God shut out of all his reckoning. But the summons came that night, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee; and the heaped barns availed nothing. So the believer is taught to hold this world’s goods with a loose hand, to lay up treasure in heaven, and above all to be rich toward God; for he that trusteth in his riches shall fall, and a sudden death may strip the covetous of every thing he called his own.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “senseless,” the parable names the covetous man a fool whose soul is required of him.

His ground brought forth plentifully, and he planned greater barns.

God required his soul that very night.

He laid up treasure for himself, and was not rich toward God.

Usage

"Like the rich fool, the covetous man reckons without God, his soul, and the world to come."

"Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in abundance."

"Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee."
